title: What Causes Mold in HVAC Systems?
h1: What Causes Mold in HVAC Systems, and How Do You Prevent It?
description: Mold in an HVAC system comes from moisture plus dust on coils, drain pans and ducts. Learn the common causes, warning signs and ways to prevent it.
quick_answer: Mold grows in HVAC systems when moisture and dust sit together long enough. The usual spots are the evaporator coil, the drain pan and ducts that sweat or leak. Clogged condensate drains, dirty filters, oversized AC units, high indoor humidity and leaky or poorly insulated ducts in hot attics are the most common causes.
body:
Your air conditioner pulls water out of the air every time it cools. That's normal, and the system is designed to drain that water away. Mold shows up when water lingers instead, and dust gives it something to feed on.

Where does mold grow in an HVAC system?

Mold usually starts in the places that get wet:

  • Evaporator coil. The indoor coil is cold and wet during cooling. Dust that gets past the filter sticks to it.
  • Drain pan. Water collects here before it leaves through the drain line. If it doesn't drain fully, it sits.
  • Condensate drain line. Algae and slime can build up inside and slow the flow.
  • Ductwork. Ducts that sweat, leak or have been wet from a roof leak can grow mold on the inside or the outside.
  • Blower and cabinet. Damp dust on the blower wheel or inside the cabinet is another common spot.

What are the most common causes?

  1. Clogged condensate drain. When the line backs up, the pan holds water. This is one of the most frequent problems we find.
  2. Dirty filters. A filter that's loaded or the wrong size lets dust onto the coil, where it stays damp.
  3. Oversized equipment. An AC that's too large runs in short bursts. It cools the air but doesn't run long enough to remove moisture, so the house stays humid.
  4. Sweating ducts. Supply ducts carry cold air through attics that can be very hot. If the insulation is torn or thin, warm attic air condenses on the outside of the duct.
  5. Leaky return ducts. Leaks can pull damp, dusty air from the attic, garage or crawl space into the system.
  6. High indoor humidity. Coastal homes with a lot of moisture in the air give mold a better chance.
  7. Long idle periods. A system that sits unused during mild months with moisture still inside can develop odors.

What are the signs of mold in your HVAC?

  • A musty or dirty-sock smell when the system turns on
  • Dark spots on registers or the ceiling around them
  • Water in the drain pan or around the furnace or air handler
  • Allergy symptoms that get worse when the system runs
  • Visible growth on the coil or inside the cabinet

Keep in mind that dark marks around ceiling registers are often dust being pulled into the ceiling texture by air leaks, not mold. An inspection can tell the difference.

How can you prevent mold in your system?

Most of prevention comes down to keeping things clean, dry and moving:

  • Check the filter monthly and replace it on schedule.
  • Have the condensate drain flushed and the pan inspected during yearly maintenance.
  • Keep indoor humidity roughly between 30 and 50 percent.
  • Set the thermostat fan to AUTO so water on the coil can drain instead of evaporating back into the house.
  • Repair torn duct insulation and seal leaky ducts, especially in the attic.
  • Ask about a UV light at the coil, which helps keep the coil surface from growing mold.

Our indoor air quality services include UV lights, humidity control and filtration upgrades.

What should you do if you find mold?

Don't spray bleach or household cleaners into your ducts or onto the coil. Bleach can damage parts, it won't reach everything, and the moisture source will still be there. Running a contaminated system can also spread spores through the house.

The right fix is to find out where the moisture comes from, clean or replace the affected parts, and correct the cause. That may mean clearing the drain, cleaning the coil and blower, cleaning and sanitizing ducts, or replacing damaged duct sections. You can learn more about duct cleaning and sanitizing on our air duct services page.

Does mold in the HVAC affect your health?

Mold can trigger allergy and asthma symptoms in sensitive people, and a musty system can make the whole house smell. If anyone in the home has ongoing breathing problems, talk with a doctor and get the system checked so you're not recirculating the problem.
faqs: Why does my AC smell musty when it turns on?
A musty smell at startup usually means moisture and growth on the coil, drain pan or ducts. A clogged drain line is a common cause. Have the system inspected before the smell gets worse.
Can I clean mold out of my air ducts myself?

Small surface cleaning at a register is fine, but cleaning inside ducts properly takes specialized equipment. Spraying chemicals into ducts can spread spores and damage the system without fixing the moisture problem.
Do UV lights kill mold in HVAC systems?
A UV light aimed at the evaporator coil helps keep mold from growing on the coil surface. It doesn't remove existing buildup or replace filtration, so it works best on a system that's already clean.
How often should the AC drain line be cleaned?
It's usually checked and flushed during yearly maintenance. Homes that have had clogs before may benefit from more frequent checks.
Do UV Lights Prevent Mold on Air Conditioner Coils?

Yes, a UV-C light aimed at the indoor coil can keep mold and bacteria from growing on the surfaces it shines on, including the coil and drain pan. It works continuously, so growth has trouble getting started. It won't clean a coil that's already heavily coated, it won't fix a drainage problem, and it only works where the light actually reaches.
